# Independent NTFS fixture

`ntfs-testfs1.img` is the published 2 MiB testfs1 image from ColinFinck/ntfs.
Source: https://github.com/ColinFinck/ntfs/tree/master/testdata
Generation script: https://github.com/ColinFinck/ntfs/blob/master/testdata/create-testfs1.sh
SHA-256: e3612c182b8010e3599b5eb93bff427c7d824e85bdc2ddbe46e378e3ba814eb9
Retrieved: 2026-10-26. License: included MIT notice.

The independent generator uses mkntfs/ntfs-3g. Expected file contents are stated
by that script, rather than generated by DaemonCore's parser implementation.
Tests read it as evidence and never mount or alter it. It validates resident,
nonresident, and sparse reads from an independently formatted NTFS volume.
It does not establish deleted-file recovery accuracy on arbitrary real disks.

The Linux NTFS validation job creates a separate image with `mkntfs`, copies
and deletes a deterministic 65,536-byte `RECOVER.BIN` through `ntfs-3g`, then
uses Sleuth Kit (`icat`) to recover and compare its exact bytes. This is a
contiguous deleted-file fixture only. An earlier fixture attempt claimed to
create a fragmented file, but allocation inspection showed its extents were
contiguous; it must not be counted as fragmentation coverage.

`prepare-nist-ntfs-dfr02.sh OUTPUT_DIR` prepares a separate fragmented-deletion
reference from NIST CFTT's DFR-02 NTFS disk image. It downloads the image from
the [NIST CFTT test-image archive](https://cfreds-archive.nist.gov/dfr-test-images.html),
pins the compressed and decompressed image hashes, and uses Sleuth Kit to
extract deleted `Bunda.txt` as the independently derived expected bytes. The
[DFR-02 setup document](https://cfreds-archive.nist.gov/dfr-images/setup-july-10-2012.pdf)
describes this as a two-fragment recovery test; the
native regression independently checks the image and expected-byte hashes,
requires non-adjacent `$DATA` runs, exports through the production recovery
path, verifies the package, and compares exact output bytes. The 1 GiB disk
image is a local test artifact and is not checked into the repository. These
references qualify one known fragmented deletion pattern; they do not qualify
reused records, alternate NTFS versions, damaged volumes, or arbitrary
real-world deletion patterns.

To prepare the reference in Ubuntu/WSL with `curl`, `bzip2`, and Sleuth Kit
installed:

```bash
bash src-tauri/tests/fixtures/prepare-nist-ntfs-dfr02.sh /path/to/fixture-dir
```

Set `DAEMONCORE_NIST_NTFS_DFR02_IMAGE` to the resulting `.dd` image and
`DAEMONCORE_NIST_NTFS_DFR02_EXPECTED` to `Bunda.txt.sleuthkit`, then run the
ignored test `ntfs_tests::exports_fragmented_deleted_ntfs_file_from_nist_dfr02_reference`
with `--ignored --exact`. The script refuses to overwrite existing artifacts.
# External reference fixtures

The exFAT validation workflow downloads a separately generated filesystem image
from [eribertomota/forensics-samples](https://github.com/eribertomota/forensics-samples)
at commit `b938bbea0d8bec5c1795433cf6227bedd9623532`. The compressed image and
decompressed image are SHA-256 pinned in `.github/workflows/validate.yml`; the
fixture is not redistributed in this repository. Upstream identifies filesystem
images as MIT licensed and requests preservation of this notice:

> Copyright 2019-2020 Joao Eriberto Mota Filho <eriberto@eriberto.pro.br>

The upstream image contains the `original-files` directory tree, then has
directories ending in `2` deleted. The test verifies the complete expected live
inventory and confirms those deleted directories are not reported as live.

The Windows validation job also runs the File Carving scanner over this same
image and compares exact candidate lengths and SHA-256 values for
`original-files/pic1/IMG_1054.JPG` and `original-files/pic1/debian.png` against
the upstream files at the same commit. The expected lengths and hashes are
recorded in the test; CI downloads the upstream originals only to pin the
reference hashes and does not redistribute them. Upstream identifies
`IMG_1054.JPG` as CC BY-SA 4.0. `debian.png` is a Debian Project logo,
Copyright 1999 SPI, identified upstream as LGPL-3+ or CC BY-SA 3.0. The
upstream README contains these notices and remains the source of licensing
terms for those files.

The Linux FAT32 validation job creates a 128 MiB image with `dosfstools`,
copies and deletes `RECOVER.BIN` with `mtools`, and requires Sleuth Kit to list
the deleted entry and recover bytes exactly equal to the original file. It
uploads the verified image and expected content as a short-lived workflow
artifact. The Windows validation job checks their SHA-256 values, then runs
both the core deleted-cluster mapper and native package exporter/verifier
against that same image and expected content. This validates the export path
on one independently formatted volume; it does not validate historical
fragmentation or deleted long-name recovery.

## BMP decode reference

`forensic-bmp-16x12.bmp` was encoded with Pillow 11.3.0, independently of the
Rust image decoder. It is a 16 × 12 RGB gradient with pixel `(x, y)` set to
`(16x, 21y, 8(x + y))`. Pillow reopened and decoded the generated file and
checked the bottom-right pixel `(240, 231, 208)` before recording the fixture.
The 630-byte encoded file has SHA-256
`f55ff8aa849bbde392a5e6e4816ca7a609b0289deab22eb1408c0592d231ce13`; the
carver regression requires that exact byte length, hash, and decoded-candidate
status. This is a controlled known-content fixture, not a broad external BMP
corpus.

## GIF decode reference

`forensic-gif-16x12.gif` was encoded by Windows GDI+ `System.Drawing`,
independently of the Rust `image` decoder. It is a 16 × 12 image with a
repeating 2 × 2 pattern: row 0 alternates black and white, and row 1 alternates
red and lime. GDI+ reopened the saved GIF and confirmed those four colors
exactly. The checked-in GIF is 854 bytes
with SHA-256
`4d1be0dda7762d6527f6aac405befa4ecabed5746dd04c9eb1f11ef1b057d170`; the
carving regression requires that exact length, hash, offset, and decoded status.
This is a controlled known-content fixture, not a broad external GIF corpus.

## Linux MD RAID 5 reference array

`make-raid01-reference-fixture.sh OUTPUT_DIR raid0|raid1` creates an
independent loop-backed Linux MD reference. RAID 0 uses three members and 64
KiB chunks; RAID 1 uses two mirrors. Both use metadata 1.0 and 8 MiB data
regions. The script writes a deterministic pattern through the active array,
reads it back through the array device, stops the array, captures each raw
member, and writes a SHA-256 manifest. The ignored Windows regression pins the
image and member hashes, then runs the production reconstruction and package
verifier against the captured members. This qualifies data order and exact
mirror agreement for these configurations, not metadata discovery, degraded
arrays, or other RAID 0/1 layouts.

Run the generator as root in Ubuntu/WSL once for each level, then set
`DAEMONCORE_RAID01_REFERENCE_DIR` to the parent directory containing `raid0`
and `raid1` before running:

```powershell
cargo test --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml --offline raid::tests::reconstructs_independent_linux_md_raid0_and_raid1_reference_arrays -- --ignored --exact
```

## Linux MD RAID 5 reference array

`make-raid5-reference-fixture.sh OUTPUT_DIR [LAYOUT]` creates three
loop-backed member devices and uses Linux MD `mdadm` with 64 KiB chunks. The
layout may be left-asymmetric, right-asymmetric, left-symmetric, or
right-symmetric (default: left-symmetric). It writes a deterministic 16 MiB
byte sequence through the active array, reads it back from the array device,
stops the array, saves the first 8 MiB of each component as a raw member image,
and records the layout and SHA-256 manifest. The array metadata is outside
those captured data extents; this validates member ordering, rotating parity,
and logical byte ordering, not metadata discovery or offset inference. The
native ignored test reads the fixture layout, reconstructs it through the
production path, and compares all output bytes to the array-device reference.
Run the generator with each layout and set `DAEMONCORE_RAID5_REFERENCE_DIR` to
the resulting absolute fixture path before running:

```powershell
cargo test --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml --offline raid::tests::reconstructs_independent_linux_md_raid5_reference_array -- --ignored --exact
```

## Linux MD RAID 6 reference array

`make-raid6-reference-fixture.sh OUTPUT_DIR [MEMBER_COUNT]` independently
creates loop-backed Linux MD RAID 6 arrays with 4–16 members, metadata 1.0,
left-symmetric layout, and 64 KiB chunks. It defaults to four members. Each
member contributes 8 MiB and the deterministic logical image fills all
`(member_count - 2) * 8 MiB` available bytes. The script reads the bytes back
from the active array, stops it, saves each member's first 8 MiB as a raw
image, and verifies a generated SHA-256 manifest. The native test
`reconstructs_independent_linux_md_raid6_reference_array` consumes that folder
through `DAEMONCORE_RAID6_REFERENCE_DIR`, reconstructs it using the production
path, and compares every output byte with the independently read array image.
Run the generator with different member counts and the test against each
resulting folder to check additional Q coefficient counts as well as
left-symmetric P/Q rotation and logical ordering. This does not qualify
missing-member recovery, metadata discovery, or other RAID 6 layouts.

The generator must run as root in Ubuntu/WSL because it creates loop devices
and Linux MD arrays. For each fixture, set
`DAEMONCORE_RAID6_REFERENCE_DIR` to its absolute path and run:

```powershell
cargo test --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml --offline raid::tests::reconstructs_independent_linux_md_raid6_reference_array -- --ignored --exact
```
